title: Eat and enjoy
hookLine: Ecclesiastes: nothing better than to eat and drink and enjoy your labor (Ecclesiastes 2:24)
last: STEADY EFFORT, AT THE RIGHT TIME.

cards: “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.” That's the Preacher's opening cry in Ecclesiastes.
Then he keeps going: the sun rises and sets, the rivers run into the sea and the sea is never full, one generation goes and another comes. A reader could expect the book to end with, so why bother.
Instead, right in the middle of all that weariness, it keeps saying something surprising. Eat. Drink.

teach.b: First, the gloom is honest. The Preacher has tried everything: building houses, planting vineyards, gathering silver and gold. Looking back on it all, he says: “all was vanity and vexation of spirit.”
He doesn't pretend work saves anyone from death, and that honesty is why what comes next carries weight.

Second, the turn, in the same chapter: “There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour.” Notice where the good is found.
Not after the work, in some distant retirement. In the labor itself. Third, the source.
The verse continues: “This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God.”

In the next chapter he says it again: to eat and drink and enjoy the good of all your labor “is the gift of God.” Enjoyment, in this book, isn't a wage you earn by working hard enough. It's a gift you're allowed to take.
Later the Preacher puts it almost as an instruction: “Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart.” Bread, wine, a table: the ordinary fruit of ordinary work.
Some Jewish communities read Ecclesiastes aloud during Sukkot, the harvest festival of booths.
A book that knows everything passes, read at a harvest feast, saying: enjoy the harvest while it's here.

how: Some Jewish communities read Ecclesiastes aloud during Sukkot, the harvest festival, and Jewish and Christian readers return to its eat-and-drink verses when they speak of enjoying the fruit of work as a gift.

games.q: you've built houses, planted vineyards, gathered silver and gold, and found it all vanity. what does the Preacher say next?

work harder until it means something.
games.why: “there is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour.”

practice: Bring to mind one fruit of your own work, a meal, a clean room, a rent payment that went through, a child's packed lunch, and notice what's good about it without reaching for the list of what's still undone.
If a cup or a piece of fruit is within reach, you can taste it now, slowly. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words.
